subject: maths
title: Chapter 8 · Test 2
summary: Chapter 8 test 2: 15 questions on probability, Venn diagrams, two-way tables, conditional and independent events, tree diagrams and counting.
body: This test covers all of Chapter 8: probability review, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, conditional probability, independent events, tree diagrams with and without replacement, and counting techniques. It has 15 multiple-choice questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Draw a quick tree, table or set of boxes on scrap paper when it helps, and check that every probability you find is between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: A bag holds 4 white, 9 grey and 3 navy socks. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is NOT grey?
questions.explanation: There are 16 socks and 7 are not grey, so P = 7/16 = 7/16.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 9/16 is the probability that it IS grey. Use the complement.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you counted colours (2 of 3 colours). Count the items, not the colours.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you divided by the 9 grey socks. A probability is out of the total, 16.

questions.prompt: The Venn diagram shows 30 people and whether they chose Piano and/or Guitar. One person is picked at random. Find P(Piano ∪ Guitar).
questions.explanation: Piano ∪ Guitar is everything inside the circles: 7 + 3 + 10 = 20, so P = 2/3.
steps: ∪ means "or": every region inside either circle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 3 is the overlap, Piano ∩ Guitar. ∪ means everything inside either circle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you left out the overlap. People in both circles are in the union too.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 10 is the whole Piano circle. Add the "Guitar only" region as well.

questions.diagram_alt: A Venn diagram with ξ = 30: Piano only 7, both 3, Guitar only 10, and 10 outside both circles

questions.prompt: Mia sits her driving test on a day when rain is forecast. P(Mia passes) = 0.6 and, independently, P(it rains) = 0.25. Find the probability that Mia passes and it rains.
questions.explanation: The events are independent, so multiply: 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.15. Adding the probabilities is the common slip.
steps: The two events don't affect each other: independent.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the probabilities. For "and" with independent events, multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 2: that is only the first event. Both must happen, so multiply by the second probability.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is only the second event. Both must happen, so multiply by the first probability.

questions.prompt: A pizza is ordered by choosing a base (4 types), a topping (5 types) and a size (2 sizes), as shown by the boxes. How many different pizzas are possible?
questions.explanation: Multiplication principle: 4 × 5 × 2 = 40. Adding gives far too few.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you added the choices. Each choice goes with every other choice — multiply.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you forgot the third choice (Size). Multiply all three boxes.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you added the size choices at the end. Every box multiplies.

questions.diagram_alt: Three boxes marked ? for the number of choices, labelled Base, Topping and Size, with multiplication signs between them

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the numbers added; the diagram shows every sum. What is the probability that the sum is 10?
questions.explanation: 3 of the 36 equally likely cells fit (4+6, 5+5, 6+4), so P = 3/36 = 1/12. The 11 sums are not equally likely.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you counted each pair once (e.g. only one of 1 + 5 and 5 + 1). Every cell is a different outcome — count all 3.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the 11 sums are not equally likely. Use the 36 cells.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you put 3 cells over 11 sums. The total is the 36 equally likely cells.

questions.diagram_alt: A 6 by 6 grid with dice values 1 to 6 along the top and side; each cell shows the sum of the two values

questions.prompt: The two-way table has some blank cells. Complete it, then find the probability that a randomly chosen person from all 100 is in the "Children" row and the "No swim" column (marked ?).
questions.explanation: Children / Swim = 45 − 27 = 18, so the ? cell = 60 − 18 = 42 and P = 42/100 = 21/50.
steps: Divide by the grand total: P = 42/100 = 21/50.

mistakes.A: Step 3: you divided by the Children row total. The person is chosen from all 100.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 18 is the Children / Swim cell. Go on to the No swim column.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 55 is the whole No swim column. You need the Children row only.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Swim, No swim, Total and rows Adults, Children, Total. Adults: Swim 27, Total 40. Children: No swim marked ?, Total 60. Total row: Swim 45, grand total 100. Other cells blank

questions.prompt: Use the two-way table. A person in the "Under 30" row is chosen at random. What is the probability that they are in the "Online" column?
questions.explanation: Given Under 30, use only that row: 33 of its 45 are Online, so P = 11/15. Dividing by the grand total ignores the condition.
steps: Given "Under 30": use only that row, 45 people.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you divided by all 100. Given "Under 30", divide by that row's total.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you divided by the Online column — that is P(Under 30 | Online). The given group is the Under 30 row.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 54/100 ignores the condition. Use only the Under 30 row.

questions.diagram_alt: A two-way table with columns Online, In store, Total and rows Under 30 (33, 12, 45), 30 or over (21, 34, 55) and Total (54, 46, 100)

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: A drawer has 7 white and 3 black socks. Two socks are taken without replacement. Find the probability that both are white.
questions.explanation: Without replacement: 7/10 × 6/9 = 7/15. Using 7/10 twice forgets that the first one is not put back.
steps: Second pick: 9 left, 6 of the right type: 6/9.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 7/10 again is WITH replacement. One has gone, so use 6/9.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you changed the top but not the bottom. Only 9 are left.
mistakes.D: Step 3: you added the branches. Along a path, multiply.

questions.prompt: Five songs are put in a playlist, and your favourite must be played last. How many different orders are possible?
questions.explanation: Fix the restricted item (1 way), then arrange the other 4: 4! = 24. 5! ignores the rule.
steps: Fill the restricted position first: 1 way.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 5! counts every order. The fixed item has only 1 place.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you subtracted from the total, which counts the orders that break the rule.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 4 items are left, but they can be arranged in many orders — use a factorial.

questions.prompt: Of 60 households, 35 have Netflix, 30 have Stan and 12 have neither. A household is chosen at random. What is the probability that it has both?
questions.explanation: 60 − 12 = 48 are in at least one group, but 35 + 30 = 65, so 65 − 48 = 17 are counted twice: they are in both. P = 17/60.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 12 is the number in neither group. Use it to find the overlap.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 48/60 is P(at least one). "Both" is only the overlap.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 35 + 30 counts the "both" people twice — compare it with 48.

steps: Addition rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.1.

mistakes.A: Step 3: dividing by P(A) gives P(B | A). The given event is B.
mistakes.B: Step 2: that is P(A ∩ B). Divide it by P(B).
mistakes.C: Step 3: you divided by P(A ∪ B). Divide by the given event, P(B).

questions.topic: Tree diagrams with and without replacement
questions.prompt: P(rain on Monday) = 0.4. If it rains on Monday, P(rain on Tuesday) = 0.6; if not, P(rain on Tuesday) = 0.2 (see the tree diagram). Find the probability that it rains on exactly one of the two days.
steps: Exactly one happens on two paths: Rain then Dry, or Dry then Rain.

mistakes.B: Step 3: that is only one path. The other order also gives exactly one — add both paths.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that path has two successes. You need exactly one.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1 − P(none) is "at least one", which includes two successes.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Rain 0.4 and Dry 0.6; after Rain, Rain 0.6 and Dry 0.4; after Dry, Rain 0.2 and Dry 0.8

questions.prompt: A basketballer takes 2 free throws and scores each with probability 0.4, independently. Find the probability that she scores at least one.

mistakes.A: Step 2: that is the chance they ALL succeed. "At least one" is 1 − P(none).
mistakes.C: Step 3: that is P(none). Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you added the probabilities. Use 1 − P(none) for "at least one".

questions.prompt: A shop gets 55% of its phones from supplier A and the rest from supplier B. 4% of A's phones are faulty and 2% of B's are faulty (see the tree diagram). A phone is found to be faulty. What is the probability it came from supplier A?
questions.explanation: P(Faulty) = 0.55 × 0.04 + 0.45 × 0.02 = 0.031. P(Supplier A and Faulty) = 0.022. So P(Supplier A | Faulty) = 0.022 ÷ 0.031 = 22/31.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 0.04 is P(Faulty | Supplier A), the condition the wrong way round. Here Faulty is given.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 0.022 is P(Supplier A and Faulty). Divide it by P(Faulty).
mistakes.D: Step 3: that is P(Supplier B | Faulty), the other branch. Use the Supplier A path on top.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram: first Supplier A 0.55 and Supplier B 0.45; after Supplier A, Faulty 0.04 and OK 0.96; after Supplier B, Faulty 0.02 and OK 0.98

questions.prompt: Two members of an 8-person team are chosen at random to be captains. What is the probability that Kai and Zara are the two chosen?
questions.explanation: Number of possible pairs = 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28, and only one of them is the pair wanted, so P = 1/28.
steps: Each pair is counted twice (in two orders), so there are 56 ÷ 2 = 28 pairs.
Only one pair is the one wanted: P = 1/28.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 8 × 7 counts ordered picks, but the pair can be picked in 2 orders. Divide by 2 first.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 2/8 is the chance that ONE particular person is chosen. Both must be chosen.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 8 × 8 lets the same person be picked twice. Count pairs of different people.
